slides.headline: A failed super-glue waited years for a choir singer to find a use for it

image.credit: Illustrative photo: wall of sticky notes / New editing editor / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.text: In the late 1960s, 3M chemist Spencer Silver was trying to make a stronger glue. He made a weaker one instead: it stuck lightly and peeled off clean. He called it "a solution waiting for a problem to solve."
In 1974, his colleague Art Fry, who sang in a church choir, was tired of paper bookmarks falling out of his hymnal. He thought of Silver's glue.

slides.text: Sometimes the invention is done. It just needs someone with a hymnal.

caption:
The sticky note started as a mistake in a lab.

In the late 1960s, 3M chemist Spencer Silver was working on a strong adhesive. What he made instead was light enough to peel away easily and could be stuck down again. He couldn't see a market for it and spent several years pitching it around the company, describing it as "a solution waiting for a problem to solve."

Then in 1974, a colleague named Art Fry sang in his church choir. His paper bookmarks kept slipping out of his hymnal. Fry remembered Silver's presentation and realized that a bookmark with a bit of that glue would stay put and lift off without damaging the page.

The product was first called Press 'n Peel. It was sold in four cities in 1977, and it became a national success in 1980 under a new name: Post-it Note. The National Inventors Hall of Fame says repositionable notes are now among the five best-selling office products in the country.

Fry spent about 40 years at 3M. Silver died in 2021 at age 80.

Source: National Inventors Hall of Fame, Associated Press
